questions.prompt: The British Isles are made up of many islands, but only two of them are large. One of the two is Great Britain. What is the other one?

options.text: England
Scotland
Ireland
Northern Ireland

questions.explanation: The two main islands of the British Isles are Great Britain and Ireland; everything else in the group is small. England and Scotland are not islands at all — they are two of the three countries that share the island of Great Britain, together with Wales. And Northern Ireland is not an island either: it is the north-east corner of the island of Ireland, and the corner that belongs to the United Kingdom. Keep asking the question that sorts these names out — is this word naming a piece of land, or a country?

questions.prompt: A student writes home from her holiday: "I have spent a whole week in Dublin without once leaving the United Kingdom." Where is she wrong?

options.text: Dublin belongs to an independent country, outside the UK.
Dublin lies inside the UK but outside the British Isles.
Dublin stands on the island of Great Britain, near Wales.
Dublin is a British city, so her sentence is quite right.

questions.explanation: Dublin is the capital of the Republic of Ireland, an independent country with its own government, and it is not one of the four constituent countries of the United Kingdom — so she left the UK the moment she landed. Dublin is nonetheless in the British Isles, because the British Isles are a group of islands and the island of Ireland is one of the two big ones. And it stands on that island, not on Great Britain: no road joins Dublin to Wales, only sea. The name Belfast is the one that goes the other way — a city on the island of Ireland that is inside the United Kingdom.

questions.prompt: The grammar box of this lesson prints two shapes one under the other: "the largest" and "the most spectacular". What decides which of the two shapes an adjective takes?

options.text: how many things are being compared with one another
how long the adjective is — how many syllables it has
whether the noun that follows it is singular or plural
whether the sentence describes a person or a place

questions.explanation: Length alone decides. A short adjective takes the ending: the largest, the oldest, the warmest — and so do the two-syllable ones in -y, which turn the y into an i: the busiest. A long adjective would break under that ending, so English puts the most in front of it instead: the most spectacular, the most captivating, the most memorable. The number of things compared decides something else entirely — with two you compare (the older of the two), with three or more you use the superlative — and neither the noun nor the subject of the sentence has any say in the matter.

questions.prompt: A guide means to tell his group "We walk to the castle", but they hear the long vowel of "first" and "church" — /ɜː/ — where the vowel of "north" should be. Which word did they hear?

options.text: wall
woke
week
work

questions.explanation: Walk is /wɔːk/, with the long vowel of north, more and warm; work is /wɜːk/, with the long vowel of first, church and world. One vowel apart, and the group has been promised a day at the office. Wall keeps the right vowel and changes the end of the word instead, woke carries the /əʊ/ of home, and week carries the long /iː/ of sheep. Note also the letter l in walk and wall: it is written and not said.

questions.prompt: A walking-tour ad calls St James's Palace the FORMER official residence of a prince. What does that one word tell a reader?

options.text: The prince used to live there and does not now.
The prince has lived there longer than anyone else.
The palace is the oldest royal building in London.
The prince owns the palace, though he rarely stays there.

questions.explanation: Former means the one before, not the one now: it puts the whole fact into the past. The prince had that palace as his official residence and he has another one today, which is exactly why a guide points the building out instead of showing you the door. Nothing in the word says anything about length of time, about the age of the building or about who owns it — an official residence comes with the post, not with the person, so the prince never owned it in the first place. One word of five letters, and the tense of a whole sentence turns with it.
